name: Novaco Anger Inventory, 25-situation English book-compatible form

source.book: David D. Burns, Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy
source.provenance: English reproductions cross-checked with the corresponding book items and scoring; no claim that a publisher-hosted first-edition facsimile was obtained.
source.normalization_notes: Contractions and typography normalized; item 17 uses the clear agreed-task wording corroborated by the NAI-25 form. Retain original US units and dated situations; explain rather than replace. Do not copy the duplicate 3 anchor or past-week instruction found in one clinical mirror; the book and NAI-25 confirm 0–4 general imagined reactions.

anchors.text: You would feel very little or no annoyance
You would feel a little irritated

items.text: You unpack an appliance you have just bought, plug it in, and discover that it does not work.
Being overcharged by a repairman who has you over a barrel.
Being singled out for correction, when the actions of others go unnoticed.
Getting your car stuck in the mud or snow.
You are talking to someone and they do not answer you.
Someone pretends to be something they are not.
While you are struggling to carry four cups of coffee to your table at a cafeteria, someone bumps into you, spilling the coffee.
You have hung up your clothes, but someone knocks them to the floor and fails to pick them up.
You are hounded by a salesperson from the moment that you walk into a store.
You have made arrangements to go somewhere with a person who backs off at the last minute and leaves you hanging.
Being joked about or teased.
Your car is stalled at a traffic light, and the guy behind you keeps blowing his horn.
You accidentally make the wrong kind of turn in a parking lot. As you get out of your car someone yells at you, "Where did you learn to drive?"
Someone makes a mistake and blames it on you.
You are trying to concentrate, but a person near you is tapping their foot.
You lend someone an important book or tool and they fail to return it.
You have had a busy day, and the person you live with starts to complain about how you forgot to do something you agreed to do.
You are trying to discuss something important with your mate or partner who is not giving you a chance to express your feelings.
You are in a discussion with someone who persists in arguing about a topic they know very little about.
Someone sticks his or her nose into an argument between you and someone else.
You need to get somewhere quickly, but the car in front of you is going 25 mph in a 40 mph zone, and you cannot pass.
Stepping on a gob of chewing gum.
Being mocked by a small group of people as you pass them.
In a hurry to get somewhere, you tear a good pair of slacks on a sharp object.
You use your last quarter to make a phone call, but you are disconnected before you finish dialing and the quarter is lost.

bands.label: Very low irritability in the book's reference ranges
Within the book's reference average range
Very high irritability in the book's reference ranges

interpretation_limits: Historical book descriptions, not contemporary population percentiles, aggression predictions or a modern full NAS-PI. Dated scenarios are retained for version consistency.
presentation_policy: Keep this single English canonical definition. Translate meaning, anchors and reference window for the conversation; record presentation language and retain the wording used. A conversational translation is not separately validated.
instructions: Imagine each situation happening to you and rate your general degree of anger or annoyance. Give one response per situation.
